description: Com base em Ciência de Dados (UFMS), nosso foco no desafio SPHEREx é otimizar a análise astronômica. Desenvolvemos uma plataforma ágil para facilitar o trabalho de cientistas da NASA e, em seguida, de entusiastas. Criamos um "Cardápio Estelar" com formatação de coordenadas por aproximação, Blink Comparator e Subtração de Imagens. O objetivo é eliminar o atrito técnico com arquivos FITS, acelerando a detecção de objetos em movimento de forma profissional.
summary:
Sky Reshearch is an early open-source prototype for a broader space-mapping platform, developed for Planet X and SPHEREx. Its current interface explores public observations through temporal image comparisons and quick-look infrared spectra. It is a first building block for a pipeline that will prepare, check and connect astronomical data while preserving its origin.

Our vision is a "Google Maps of space" with different paths for different users: the public could explore and learn, enthusiasts could follow objects, data scientists could analyze observations, and researchers and universities could investigate and teach. Observation and Research modes support different levels of detail.

The next intended delivery is an initial 3D Milky Way map, with nearby galaxies presented in a simple 2D overview that opens into 3D exploration. A future "space GPS" could connect positions and motion over time. These are development goals, not completed capabilities. Community access and feedback already help shape the project; future contributions could add sources, modules and scientific validation.
details:
VISION AND CURRENT STAGE

Sky Reshearch is a small prototype and the first building block of an open-source space-mapping platform. The long-term vision is a "Google Maps of space": an accessible environment for locating objects, understanding their spatial context and exploring how positions change over time. The conceptual map and future navigation experience are proposals, not a completed scientific map or operational positioning system.

RESPONSE TO PLANET X AND SPHEREx

The present prototype addresses the challenge through public astronomical observations, temporal image comparison and infrared exploration. The interface includes guided targets, a star map, an image laboratory and a quick-look spectral workspace. Temporal SPHEREx comparisons use separate spectral-image products from different epochs. The combined DR1 all-sky cube supports channel and exploratory spectral views and is not treated as separate epochs. The guided targets are Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Availability depends on archive services and coverage.

THE DATA FOUNDATION

The broader pipeline remains in development. It aims to collect and standardize observations, assess quality, identify missing or incompatible information and connect sources while retaining provenance. Coordinate systems, epochs, units and quality indicators must be compatible before observations can be meaningfully related. The current backend uses Python, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and Pillow. The frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Public IRSA/SPHEREx products and supporting DSS and infrared surveys provide observational material.

WHO COULD USE IT AND WHY

For the general public, the intended entry point is a familiar question, such as understanding an object mentioned in the news or exploring our cosmic neighborhood, rather than requiring coordinates. Enthusiasts could follow objects and explore related observations. Astronomy data scientists could analyze organized datasets. Researchers and universities could connect evidence, develop analyses, teach and contribute methods. The existing Observation and Research modes expose different levels of detail. These design choices still need testing with different users.

NEXT DELIVERY: AN INITIAL 3D MAP

The next intended delivery is a first 3D representation of the Milky Way based on a limited, identified set of objects and available information, alongside access to nearby galaxies. A simple 2D overview would help users find and select a galaxy, which would open into 3D exploration with associated data. Scientific positions, illustrative structure, approximate distances and display scales must be distinguished. The conceptual visuals describe this future experience.

LONG-TERM HORIZON: A "SPACE GPS"

The term expresses a vision of orientation and temporal exploration. A possible future example is consulting the Moon's calculated position for a chosen time and observing location. Updating a calculated position is different from receiving live observations, and refresh rates depend on source availability. A later application could contextualize validated information about near-Earth-object approaches. Support for disaster prevention would require specialized data, scientific validation and response processes. It is not an implemented forecasting or warning capability.

RELATED TOOLS AND CREATIVE APPROACH

Aladin, WorldWide Telescope, NASA Eyes and JPL Horizons illustrate related approaches to sky visualization, education and positions over time. They are references for the vision, not claimed current integrations. Our intended contribution is an open workflow connecting data preparation, cross-source exploration and progressively deeper interaction. The creative proposal lies in how these components could work together for different audiences.

OPEN SOURCE AND COMMUNITY

The repository declares an MIT license for the code; external data retain their own usage and citation requirements. Open source provides a way for the community to extend the project with connectors, modules, translations, accessibility improvements and scientific review. Reusable contributions could multiply development capacity, with documentation and review supporting quality. At this early stage, simply accessing the prototype and sharing feedback is already a valuable contribution.

LIMITATIONS

The prototype does not automatically detect or confirm Planet X, measure proper motion or establish a discovery. Blink comparisons are qualitative. Quick-look spectra are exploratory surface-brightness extractions, not calibrated point-source photometry. Coverage, alignment, calibration and service availability affect interpretation. Alternative surveys are labeled by origin. The future 3D map, cross-source pipeline and "space GPS" require further development and validation.

AI AND MEDIA DISCLOSURE

OpenAI Codex and Google Gemini assisted with development, debugging, ideation, documentation and submission preparation. Visual Studio Code served as the development environment. OpenAI ImageGen produced the conceptual galaxy illustrations used in presentation media; these are labeled as AI-generated and do not represent observational evidence or a working scientific map. The English pitch uses the macOS Samantha synthetic voice and AI-assisted editing and captions. Astronomical images and spectra returned by the application come from the observational sources identified in the project.
